title: What is Machine Learning?
simple_explanation: ML learns patterns from data to make predictions.
short_detail: ML learns patterns from training data. A core subset of AI where systems learn to perform tasks and improve by identifying patterns in data, rather than following explicit rules.
detailed_explanation: ML learns patterns from training data. Machine Learning (ML) is a core subset of AI where systems learn to perform tasks and improve by identifying patterns in data, rather than following explicit rules. Instead of programming rules, ML algorithms learn from examples. Major paradigms include supervised learning (learning from labeled examples), unsupervised learning (finding patterns in unlabeled data), and reinforcement learning (learning through trial and error with rewards). ML encompasses many algorithms: linear regression, decision trees, neural networks, support vector machines, and more. Modern ML is dominated by deep learning (neural networks with many layers), which has achieved breakthrough performance across domains.

title: Supervised Learning

detailed_explanation: Supervised learning uses labeled examples. Supervised Learning is a machine learning paradigm where models learn from labeled training data — input-output pairs where the correct answer is provided. The model learns to map inputs to outputs by minimizing the difference between its predictions and the labels. Supervised learning encompasses classification (predicting categories) and regression (predicting continuous values). It requires large amounts of labeled data, which can be expensive to obtain. Applications include image classification, spam detection, medical diagnosis, and translation. Supervised learning is the most common ML paradigm but is limited by the need for labels — motivating research into self-supervised and unsupervised approaches.

title: Unsupervised Learning

Unsupervised Learning is a machine learning paradigm where models discover patterns and structures from unlabeled data without explicit guidance on correct outputs. Unlike supervised learning (with labels) and reinforcement learning (with rewards), unsupervised learning identifies inherent structure in data. Common techniques include clustering (grouping similar data points), dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE), and density estimation. Applications include customer segmentation, anomaly detection, feature learning, and data exploration. Unsupervised learning is valuable when labeled data is scarce or expensive. While less directly applicable than supervised learning, unsupervised techniques are essential for understanding data and feature engineering.

title: Reinforcement Learning

detailed_explanation: Reinforcement learning uses actions and rewards. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a type of machine learning where an agent learns to make decisions by interacting with an environment, receiving rewards for good actions and penalties for bad ones. The agent learns a policy (strategy) that maximizes cumulative reward over time. RL differs from supervised learning (learning from labeled examples) and unsupervised learning (finding patterns in unlabeled data). RL applications include game playing (AlphaGo, AlphaStar), robotics, autonomous vehicles, and AI alignment (RLHF). Challenges include sample efficiency, reward design, and stability. RL is powerful but complex — requiring careful environment design and reward shaping.

title: Overfitting

detailed_explanation: Overfitting causes poor generalization to new examples. Overfitting and Underfitting are two fundamental failure modes in machine learning representing the bias-variance tradeoff. Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training data (including noise) instead of learning general patterns — it performs excellently on training data but poorly on new data. Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns — it performs poorly on both training and new data. The goal is to find the sweet spot: a model complex enough to capture patterns but simple enough to generalize. Techniques to address overfitting include regularization, dropout, early stopping, and more data. Techniques to address underfitting include more complex models, more features, and longer training.

title: Cross-Validation
simple_explanation: Cross-validation tests performance across multiple training-validation splits.
short_detail: Cross-validation evaluates performance across different splits. A technique for assessing how AI models generalize to independent datasets by partitioning data into training and validation subsets multiple times.
detailed_explanation: Cross-validation evaluates performance across different splits. Cross-validation is a statistical technique for assessing how AI models will generalize to independent datasets. The most common form, k-fold cross-validation, partitions data into k subsets, trains the model on k-1 subsets, validates on the remaining subset, and repeats k times. This provides a more robust estimate of model performance than a single train-test split, reduces variance in performance estimates, and makes efficient use of limited data. Variants include stratified k-fold (preserving class distributions), leave-one-out, and time-series cross-validation (respecting temporal order).

Regularization is a set of techniques that prevent a model from overfitting by adding a penalty for complexity, forcing it to learn broader, generalizable patterns. Common regularization techniques include: L1/L2 regularization (penalizing large weights), dropout (randomly disabling neurons during training), early stopping (halting training before overfitting), data augmentation (artificially expanding training data), and weight decay. Regularization is essential for building models that generalize well to new data. The right amount of regularization is task-dependent — too little leads to overfitting, too much leads to underfitting.

title: Deep Learning
simple_explanation: A type of AI that uses many layers of artificial neurons to learn complicated patterns from data — the technology behind modern AI breakthroughs.
short_detail: A subset of machine learning based on multi-layered neural networks that progressively extract complex features from raw data.
detailed_explanation: Deep Learning is a subset of machine learning based on artificial neural networks with multiple layers (hence 'deep'). These layers progressively extract increasingly abstract features from raw data — from simple edges in images to complex semantic concepts. Deep learning has revolutionized AI since around 2012, achieving breakthrough performance in computer vision, speech recognition, natural language processing, and game playing. Key architectures include CNNs for images, RNNs and Transformers for sequences, and GANs for generation. Deep learning's success is enabled by large datasets, powerful GPUs, and algorithmic advances like backpropagation and attention mechanisms.

title: Gradient Descent
simple_explanation: The algorithm that teaches AI by repeatedly adjusting it in the direction that reduces its errors — like rolling a ball downhill to find the lowest point.
short_detail: An iterative optimization algorithm that minimizes a loss function by updating model parameters in the direction of steepest descent.
detailed_explanation: Gradient Descent is an iterative optimization algorithm that minimizes a loss function by updating model parameters in the direction of steepest descent (negative gradient). At each step, parameters are adjusted by: parameter = parameter - learning_rate × gradient. Variants include batch gradient descent (uses all data), stochastic gradient descent (SGD, uses one example), and mini-batch gradient descent (uses small batches). Advanced optimizers like Adam, RMSProp, and AdaGrad build on gradient descent with adaptive learning rates and momentum. Gradient descent is the foundation of neural network training, enabling models to learn from data.

title: Learning Rate
simple_explanation: How big of a step the AI takes when learning — too big and it overshoots, too small and it takes forever to learn.
short_detail: A critical hyperparameter controlling the size of optimization steps during training, with values that are too high causing instability and too low causing slow convergence.
detailed_explanation: Learning Rate is a critical hyperparameter controlling the size of optimization steps during training. At each step, parameters are updated by: parameter = parameter - learning_rate × gradient. Too high a learning rate causes instability (parameters overshoot optimal values, loss oscillates or diverges). Too low a learning rate causes slow convergence (training takes forever) and risk of getting stuck in local minima. Learning rate schedules (decay over time), warmup (start small, increase), and adaptive methods (Adam adjusts per-parameter) help manage learning rate. Finding the right learning rate is crucial for successful training.

title: Backpropagation
simple_explanation: The process of teaching a neural network by showing it its mistakes and adjusting it from the end back to the beginning.
short_detail: The fundamental algorithm for training neural networks by calculating and propagating error gradients backward to update weights.
detailed_explanation: Backpropagation (backward propagation of errors) is the fundamental algorithm for training neural networks. It works by: (1) making a forward pass to compute the output, (2) calculating the error (loss) between prediction and target, (3) computing gradients of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule of calculus, propagating these gradients backward through the network, and (4) updating weights using an optimizer like gradient descent. Backpropagation enables efficient training of deep networks by reusing computations, making modern deep learning possible.

title: Transfer Learning
simple_explanation: Taking what an AI learned from one task and applying it to a different but related task — saving time and data.
short_detail: A technique where knowledge from one task is applied to a related task, reducing data and compute requirements.
detailed_explanation: Transfer Learning is a technique where knowledge from one task (the source task) is applied to a related task (the target task), reducing data and compute requirements. Instead of training from scratch, models are pre-trained on a large dataset (source task), then fine-tuned on a smaller dataset for the specific task (target task). Transfer learning is the foundation of modern AI — GPT is pre-trained on text, then fine-tuned for specific applications; image models are pre-trained on ImageNet, then fine-tuned for specific vision tasks. Benefits include: reduced data needs, faster training, and better performance (especially when target data is limited). Transfer learning enables efficient creation of specialized models.

title: Fine-tuning
simple_explanation: Taking a general-purpose AI and training it more on specific data to make it an expert at a particular task.
short_detail: The process of taking a pre-trained AI model and further training it on a specific dataset or task to improve its performance for a particular use case.
detailed_explanation: Fine-tuning is the process of taking a pre-trained AI model and further training it on a specific dataset or task to improve its performance for a particular use case. Instead of training from scratch (expensive, data-intensive), fine-tuning adapts an existing model's knowledge to new domains. Techniques range from full fine-tuning (updating all parameters) to parameter-efficient methods like LoRA and adapters (updating small subsets). Fine-tuning is how general foundation models become specialized tools — a general LLM becomes a medical assistant, code helper, or customer service bot through fine-tuning on relevant data.

title: Self-Supervised Learning
simple_explanation: AI that teaches itself from unlabeled data by creating its own practice problems — like learning language by predicting the next word.
short_detail: A learning paradigm where models learn from unlabeled data by creating their own supervision signals through pretext tasks.
detailed_explanation: Self-Supervised Learning is a learning paradigm where models learn from unlabeled data by creating their own supervision signals through pretext tasks. Unlike supervised learning (which requires labeled data) and unsupervised learning (which finds patterns without explicit objectives), self-supervised learning defines a task from the data itself. Examples: predicting the next word in text (GPT), masking and reconstructing parts of input (BERT), or predicting rotated versions of images. Self-supervised learning has enabled training on massive unlabeled datasets (the entire internet), producing foundation models with broad capabilities. It's the dominant pre-training approach for modern AI.

title: Softmax Function
simple_explanation: A math function that turns AI's raw scores into probabilities that add up to 100% — showing how confident the AI is in each possible answer.
short_detail: A mathematical function used at the output layer of neural networks to convert a vector of raw scores (logits) into a normalized probability distribution.
detailed_explanation: The Softmax Function is a mathematical function used at the output layer of neural networks to convert a vector of raw scores (logits) into a normalized probability distribution. Softmax exponentiates each score and divides by the sum of all exponentiated scores, ensuring all outputs are positive and sum to 1. This allows the outputs to be interpreted as probabilities. For example, in classification, softmax converts raw scores for each class into probabilities, with the highest probability indicating the predicted class. Softmax is differentiable, enabling backpropagation. It's fundamental to classification tasks and language models (where it produces the probability distribution over the vocabulary for next-token prediction).

title: Transformer
simple_explanation: The AI architecture behind ChatGPT and modern language models — processes all words at once using attention, revolutionizing AI since 2017.
short_detail: A revolutionary deep learning architecture that uses self-attention mechanisms to process entire sequences of data simultaneously, forming the foundation of modern LLMs.
detailed_explanation: The Transformer is a revolutionary deep learning architecture introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' that uses self-attention mechanisms to process entire sequences of data simultaneously. Unlike RNNs (which process sequentially), Transformers process all tokens in parallel, enabling much faster training and better handling of long-range dependencies. The Transformer architecture consists of encoder and decoder blocks, each with multi-head self-attention and feed-forward layers. Transformers are the foundation of modern LLMs (GPT, BERT, T5, Llama, Claude) and have revolutionized not just NLP but also computer vision (Vision Transformers), audio processing, and more. The Transformer is arguably the most important AI architecture of the past decade.

title: Attention Mechanism
simple_explanation: A method that helps AI pay attention to the most important parts of what it's looking at, like how you focus on the key words in a sentence.
short_detail: A technique that allows AI models to focus on the most relevant parts of input data when processing information, enabling them to understand context.
detailed_explanation: The Attention Mechanism is a technique that enables AI models to dynamically focus on different parts of the input when producing output. Introduced in the context of neural machine translation, attention allows models to weigh the importance of different input elements (like words in a sentence) when generating each part of the output. Self-attention, where elements attend to other elements in the same sequence, is the foundation of Transformer architectures. Attention mechanisms have been crucial to advances in language understanding, translation, and many other AI tasks.

title: Embedding
simple_explanation: Converting words, images, or other data into lists of numbers that capture their meaning — so similar things have similar numbers.
short_detail: A dense, multi-dimensional vector representation of data that captures its semantic meaning for similarity search.
detailed_explanation: An Embedding is a dense, multi-dimensional vector representation of data that captures its semantic meaning. Words, sentences, images, or other data are mapped to points in a high-dimensional space where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity. Embeddings enable powerful operations like semantic search (finding conceptually similar items), clustering (grouping related data), and classification. Modern embeddings are learned through training neural networks on large datasets, capturing nuanced relationships — for example, 'king' - 'man' + 'woman' ≈ 'queen' in word embedding space. Embeddings are foundational to modern AI applications.

title: Token
simple_explanation: The basic chunks that AI breaks text into — could be a word, part of a word, or even a single character.
short_detail: The basic unit of text that AI language models process, where text is broken down into smaller pieces.
detailed_explanation: A Token is the basic unit of text that AI language models process. Text is broken down (tokenized) into tokens before being fed to the model. Tokens can be words, subwords, characters, or byte sequences, depending on the tokenizer. Modern tokenizers like BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) and WordPiece balance vocabulary size and coverage — common words are single tokens, rare words are split into subword tokens. Token count matters because: (1) models have context window limits (measured in tokens), (2) API pricing is based on token count, and (3) different languages have different token efficiencies (English is more token-efficient than Chinese, for example). Understanding tokens is essential for effective AI use.

title: Hyperparameter
simple_explanation: Settings you choose before training an AI — like how fast it learns or how many examples it looks at at once — that control the training process.
short_detail: A configuration setting external to the model that controls the training process (e.g., learning rate, batch size), set before training begins.
detailed_explanation: Hyperparameters are configuration settings external to the model that control the training process, set before training begins. Unlike model parameters (weights learned from data), hyperparameters are chosen by practitioners. Examples include learning rate, batch size, number of layers, dropout rate, and optimizer choice. Hyperparameter tuning — finding optimal values — is crucial for model performance but can be expensive (each configuration requires full training). Techniques include grid search (trying all combinations), random search, Bayesian optimization, and population-based training. The distinction between hyperparameters and parameters is fundamental to understanding ML workflows.

title: Data Augmentation
simple_explanation: Creating more training examples by slightly modifying existing ones — like flipping images or rewording text — to help AI learn better.
short_detail: A technique used to artificially increase the size and diversity of a training dataset by applying label-preserving transformations to existing data.
detailed_explanation: Data Augmentation is a technique used to artificially increase the size and diversity of a training dataset by applying transformations that preserve the original labels. For images, this includes rotations, flips, crops, color adjustments, and more sophisticated techniques like mixup and cutout. For text, augmentation includes synonym replacement, back-translation, and paraphrasing. Augmentation helps models generalize better, reduces overfitting, and is particularly valuable when labeled data is scarce. The key challenge is ensuring transformations are semantically valid — modifications shouldn't change the underlying meaning or label.

title: Hallucination
simple_explanation: When an AI confidently makes things up — stating false information as if it were true.
short_detail: When an AI model generates confident but incorrect or fabricated information, presenting it as factual.
detailed_explanation: Hallucination occurs when an AI model generates confident but incorrect or fabricated information, presenting it as factual. LLMs are particularly prone to hallucination because they're optimized for generating plausible text, not necessarily accurate text. Types include intrinsic hallucination (contradicting provided context), extrinsic hallucination (adding unsupported information), and factual hallucination (stating false facts). Hallucination is problematic in high-stakes applications (medical, legal, financial). Mitigation techniques include retrieval-augmented generation (grounding in real sources), uncertainty quantification, verification tools, and user education about AI limitations.

title: Generative AI
simple_explanation: AI that creates new content — text, images, music, code — by learning patterns from existing examples.
short_detail: AI systems designed to create new, original content (text, images, code) by learning the underlying patterns of existing data.
detailed_explanation: Generative AI refers to AI systems designed to create new, original content (text, images, audio, video, code) by learning the underlying patterns of existing data. Unlike discriminative AI (which classifies or predicts), generative AI produces novel outputs. Major approaches include: autoregressive models (GPT for text), diffusion models (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion for images), GANs, and variational autoencoders. Generative AI has exploded since 2022 with ChatGPT, enabling applications from content creation to code generation to scientific discovery. It raises important questions about creativity, copyright, misinformation, and the future of human work.
